# The Weight of Knowing

Rajan is a 37-year-old South Asian psychologist who has spent the better part of his career helping others make sense of their most shattering experiences. There is a particular cruelty, he sometimes thinks, in the fact that he now sits on the other side of that equation — though he would never say this out loud, not to his wife, not to his colleagues, and certainly not to his patients.

Fourteen months ago, Rajan was attending an international mental health conference in a major European city. He was presenting a paper on trauma-informed care — a detail that has not escaped him. He was standing near the hotel lobby when the first explosion tore through the entrance. What followed were eleven minutes that he can reconstruct with a precision that feels less like memory and more like footage he cannot stop playing. The smell of burning fabric and plaster. A woman near him whose mouth was open but whose voice he could not hear over the ringing. A man lying face down on the marble floor, completely still. Rajan pulled two people behind a overturned service cart and pressed his body against theirs until the shooting stopped. Three people in that lobby did not survive.

He flew home four days later, after police interviews and a night in a hospital being treated for a laceration on his forearm. His wife, Priya, met him at the airport and held him for a long time. He told her he was fine. He believed it, briefly.

Within three weeks, he stopped sleeping through the night. He would wake at two or three in the morning with his heart hammering, convinced he could smell smoke, convinced the bedroom door was wrong somehow — too exposed. He began checking the locks in their home three and four times before bed. He mapped exits in every building he entered, including his own office, where he has practiced for nine years. He knows, intellectually, what he is doing. He knows the name for it. That knowledge offers him almost nothing.

The harder thing — the thing he has not fully admitted even to himself — is what has happened to his work. Rajan sits with patients who have survived violence, accidents, assault, and he finds that the careful professional distance he once maintained has collapsed entirely. When a patient describes a moment of helplessness, something in his chest seizes. He has learned to keep his face neutral. He is very good at keeping his face neutral. But he leaves sessions exhausted in a way that feels cellular, and he has begun quietly reducing his caseload, citing administrative pressures to his practice manager.

He avoids the news with a discipline that borders on ritual. He has not returned to any conference since the attack. He declined an invitation to speak at a symposium in London and told the organizers it was a scheduling conflict. Priya knows this was not true. She has started asking careful questions in the evenings, the kind of questions he recognizes as gentle clinical probes, and he both loves her for it and finds himself deflecting with a fluency that embarrasses him.

There are moments — driving to work, standing in the kitchen making tea — when the lobby comes back without warning. Not as a thought but as a full sensory reinstatement: the ringing, the stillness of that man on the floor, the particular quality of the light through the shattered glass. Rajan has a word for this too. He has written about this phenomenon in peer-reviewed journals.

He describes himself to Priya as "still processing." He describes himself to himself, in his more honest moments, as someone who is managing — which he understands is not the same thing as recovering. He continues to see his patients each day, to listen carefully, to hold their stories with both hands. He is not sure anyone around him understands how much effort that is taking right now. He is not sure he wants them to.
